name: Sidecar — the outside-processing quote desk for job shops
one_liner: For the estimator or buyer at a 10-80 person CNC/fab job shop, Sidecar is an email agent that gets the outside-processing price (heat treat, anodize, plating, coating) before the customer quote goes out: it reads the print, builds a spec-correct vendor RFQ, emails every approved processor, chases them on a cadence, and returns a dated, side-by-side price/lead-time/minimum card the estimator can drop straight into the quote.
problem: Most job-shop quotes for aerospace/medical/defence work include at least one outside process — heat treat, anodize, plate, passivate, powder coat. The estimator cannot price the job until the finisher comes back, and finishers are small (two-thirds of US plating shops have under 20 employees per IBISWorld-derived figures) with no rate card and no portal. So the estimator either emails three vendors and waits days — one job-shop guide names "waiting on outside-process prices" as the explicit bottleneck against a 24-48 hour quote target (netray.co) — or drops in a remembered number. That guess is where the margin goes: lot minimums, rack/setup charges, freight and certificate costs are the specific items the trade sources name as commonly missed or stale (mfgcalcs.com, uptool.com). Outside processing shows up in a meaningful share of jobs (one scheduling source: 30-40% of jobs at many job shops; one machining firm says ~65% of its parts), and the whole loop — spec extraction, vendor email, chasing, transcribing the reply — is done by hand in Outlook. The new AI quoting wave (Paperless Parts Wingman, Uptool at $195/mo, Forgepoint's "Frank", $9.8M seed from Primary + a16z speedrun, Oct 2026) all automates the *customer-facing* side of the quote and leaves this upstream dependency to the human.
target_customer: Owner/GM or head estimator at a 10-80 employee CNC machining or sheet-metal job shop doing build-to-print work with quality flowdowns (AS9100 / ISO 13485 shops are the sweet spot, because the spec callout — AMS 2700, MIL-A-8625 Type II Class 2, AMS-H-6875 — has to be flowed to the processor exactly). Buyer is the owner or GM; daily user is the estimator or buyer who already does this by email. Secondary buyer: the purchasing manager at a 50-150 person contract manufacturer with 10-30 approved processors on its AVL.
why_now: Three things changed in the last 12-18 months. (1) Models are now reliably good at pulling spec callouts, revisions and quality clauses off PDF prints — Paperless Parts' Wingman 2.0 ships surface-finish, weld-symbol and spec extraction (10,000+ spec types) as a product feature, so the extraction half of this is a solved commodity rather than research (https://www.paperlessparts.com/press/paperless-parts-launches-wingman-2-0-to-bring-deeper-print-intelligence-to-the-quoting-workflow/). (2) The money has arrived in the exact adjacent lane and validated the buyer: Forgepoint raised $9.8M seed led by Primary Venture Partners and a16z speedrun in Oct 2026 for an AI quoting rep for metalworking, and Uptool raised $6M seed in Feb 2026 — both selling to the same estimator, both aimed at the customer-facing quote, neither at the vendor-facing one (https://techfundingnews.com/forgepoint-raises-9-8m-from-primary-and-a16z-speedrun-to-put-ai-on-the-factory-quote-desk/). (3) Investor signals point straight here: YC W27 "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (Brad Flora, https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#the-15-an-hour-expert) describes exactly this — give an ordinary office person an agent and they do the specialist's spec-flowdown job; a16z Big Ideas 2026 "The renaissance of the American factory" (Erin Price-Wright) and "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" (Joe Schmidt, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-2/) argue the next wave of AI value is in exactly these 20-person industrial back offices. The bookmark that triggered it: @hemanthug's twentyfour26 post about 48-hour CNC turnaround — the thing that makes 48 hours impossible for everyone else is the outside-process loop.
comparables: Paperless Parts (paperlessparts.com) — the category leader for job-shop quoting; Wingman 2.0 extracts specs and callouts from prints, but its job ends at building the customer quote; it does not go out to the processor and get a price. Gap: the vendor-facing leg. Uptool (uptool.com, $6M seed Feb 2026, from $195/mo) — AI RFQ inbox and quoting for shops under 100 people; publishes content about outside processes but sells estimator-side quoting, not vendor RFQ orchestration. Forgepoint "Frank" (forgepoint.ai, $9.8M seed Oct 2026, Primary + a16z speedrun) — closest in spirit and the biggest competitive threat: an AI inside-sales rep that reads inbound RFQs, asks the *customer* for missing specs, drafts and follows up on quotes; it points the agent outward at buyers, not upward at the shop's own supply chain, and explicitly serves coating/heat-treat shops as sellers rather than machine shops as buyers. Steelhead ($84M from Mainsail, 250+ shops, gosteelhead.com) — ERP/MES for the finisher; runs the processor's business, not the machine shop's buying of it. Bizowie, JobPack, ProShop, E2 — ERPs that record a subcontract operation and its expected cost on the routing, but the price still has to be typed in by a human who got it by email. Buyer-side RFQ tools (AuraVMS $4.99/user/mo, oboloo, Axya) — generic multi-vendor RFQ collection, no print reading, no spec flowdown, no manufacturing process logic. Verified gap: across 12 deep-research calls I found no product that reads a print, generates the spec-correct processor RFQ, emails the AVL, chases, and returns comparable dated prices with minimums and freight.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. ~5,000 US coating/plating/heat-treat establishments (Census NAICS 332811/332813-derived) on the supply side; the buyer side is the ~20,000+ US CNC/fab job shops, of which the serviceable segment — shops with 10-80 employees doing spec-flowdown work — is plausibly 5,000-8,000. Shops already pay for software in this band: Anoplex publishes $150-$375/mo tiers, Uptool starts at $195/mo, a third-party listing puts Steelhead around $500/mo (unconfirmed by the vendor), Paperless Parts is quote-only with third-party listings at $300-$750/mo that the vendor says are inaccurate. So $300-$600/mo per shop is a defensible price point with existing budget precedent, implying a $20-50M ARR ceiling on the wedge alone before expanding into the OSP purchase order, the parts-at-vendor chase and the cert-return check. The honest risk: this is a modest TAM for the wedge, and the venture case depends on expanding from "get the price" into owning the whole outside-processing lane.
risks: 1) Forgepoint or Paperless Parts adds a "get outside-process pricing" button as a feature inside the quote they already own — this is a feature-shaped wedge sitting next to two funded incumbents, and the defence has to be the vendor-side network effect (processors that answer Sidecar RFQs faster because the format is clean) built fast. 2) The processors may simply not answer faster for a nicely formatted email; if finisher response latency is driven by their own estimator being underwater, Sidecar makes the shop's chasing cheaper but does not shorten the clock, which halves the pitch. 3) Selling to 20-person shops is slow, in-person, trade-show-shaped work, and this builder is a nights-and-weekends operator in a different time zone from the Midwest shops that buy this. 4) I could not find a defensible number for OSP spend as a share of job-shop COGS, so the ROI story must be built from the shop's own POs during the pilot rather than from an industry statistic.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That the estimator's real blocker is the *waiting and chasing*, not just the typing — i.e. that a shop will pay to have the vendor loop run for them rather than just using a stale rate table. Most fragile: shops may be perfectly happy guessing from history. 2) That processors (small, email-driven, no portal) will actually reply to an agent-generated RFQ at a decent rate without a prior relationship — the whole output depends on their response. 3) That the price is actually unconfirmed often enough to matter: if 70% of OSP lines are repeat parts with known prices, the addressable moments per week collapse. 4) That spec flowdown accuracy (AMS/MIL callouts, class/type, approved-source restrictions) can be made reliable enough that a buyer trusts the generated RFQ without re-reading the print — if they re-read it anyway, the time saving evaporates.
first_customers: Ten shops, found in three places. (a) AS9100-certified machine shops with 10-80 employees, filterable by certificate from the IAQG OASIS registry and by state — start with the Midwest (Ohio, Michigan, Indiana) and Southern California aerospace clusters, cold email the owner with a free teardown of one of their own real prints. (b) r/CNC, r/Machinists and the Practical Machinist "Shop Management" forum — post the teardown, not the product. (c) Regional events where estimators actually are: PMPA and NTMA chapter meetings, and the Fabtech / IMTS floor. The single best opening line is the free one-off: "send me one print with a heat-treat or anodize callout and the names of three processors you use, and I'll send you back the three quotes." That is a service first, software second, which is the right shape for this buyer.
validation_test: This week, concierge it by hand for five shops. Get five real prints with outside-process callouts (ask in r/CNC and by cold email to AS9100 shops), hand-extract the spec with a model, send a clean RFQ to each shop's three named processors from a Sidecar address, chase at 48h and 96h, and return a dated comparison card. Pass signal: at least 3 of 5 shops say the card was faster or more accurate than what they'd have done, AND at least 2 of 5 say yes to "$400/month for this running automatically from your Outlook" after seeing it. Harder pass: one shop prepays a $500 pilot month. Fail signal: shops say "we just use our rate table for that", or processor reply rate to the agent RFQs is under 50% in four days — in which case the pain is in the shop's memory, not in the vendor loop, and the idea should pivot to maintaining a dated vendor rate book instead.
build_plan:
Narrowest first sellable version — "get me the outside-process price", nothing else. Stack: TypeScript + a hosted inbox (Postmark or Gmail API), Claude/GPT with vision for print reading, Postgres, plain server-rendered UI. No ERP integration in v1.

1. Intake by forward. The estimator forwards the customer RFQ (PDF print + email) to rfq@theirshop.sidecar.app. No login, no install, no ERP connector — that is the single biggest adoption unlock for a 20-person shop.
2. Spec extraction with a confidence gate. Model pulls process callouts (AMS 2700, MIL-A-8625 Type II Cl.2, AMS-H-6875, RoHS/REACH notes), material, alloy/condition, quantity, part dimensions for surface-area estimation, masking notes, revision, and any approved-source restriction. Anything below threshold is shown to the estimator as a one-screen confirm before a single email goes out. This is the trust moment; do not skip it.
3. Vendor fan-out. Shop pastes its approved processor list once (name, email, processes, any known minimums). Agent sends each one a clean, identical RFQ email with the spec quoted verbatim, the quantity, the due date and the print attached. Chase at 48h and 96h, then stop and tell the estimator who went dark.
4. The comparison card. Parse replies (free-text email, the real-world case) into price per part, lot minimum, setup/rack charge, freight, lead time, and certs included — each line dated and with the vendor's raw email one click away. Copy-to-clipboard as a quote line, and a PDF.
5. The rate book, built as a by-product. Every answered RFQ writes a dated price into that shop's private vendor rate book, so the second quarter of use answers common jobs instantly without emailing anyone. This is the retention mechanic and the start of the moat.
6. Pricing and sale: $400/month flat for one shop, unlimited RFQs, first month as a paid pilot at $500 with the founder manually backstopping every extraction.

Cut from v1: ERP/MES integration, the purchase order, parts-at-vendor tracking, cert-return checking, any vendor-facing portal or login, multi-shop analytics, mobile app, and any attempt to price the machining itself — that is Paperless Parts' and Uptool's ground and walking onto it loses.
launch_post:
Your machining quote is sitting there because the anodizer hasn't emailed back.

Sidecar reads the print, pulls the spec (MIL-A-8625 Ty II Cl 2), emails all four of your processors, chases them, and hands you one card: price, lot minimum, freight, lead time, dated.

Stop guessing $1.85/pc.
reasoning:
Tonight's bookmarks were mostly developer-tool noise — a Cursor deploy launch, a codebase-cleanup skill, a security guide — which is a crowded lane and close to several past ideas (SkillProof, SkillPeek, Ledger, Doublecheck). The one bookmark pointing at a real industrial workflow was @hemanthug's twentyfour26 post about autonomous CNC machining with 48-hour turnaround. That reframed the question usefully: what actually makes 48 hours impossible for the 20,000 ordinary job shops? The answer that survived research is the outside-processing loop — the days a shop waits for a heat treater or anodizer to price a job before it can price its own.

Sidecar beat the alternatives on three things. First, the gap is verified rather than assumed: I found the funded players (Forgepoint $9.8M, Uptool $6M, Paperless Parts, Steelhead $84M) and they all point the agent at the *customer* side of the quote or at the finisher's own shop floor. Twelve deep-research and sharpening calls could not surface a product that reads the print, builds the spec-correct processor RFQ, emails the approved vendor list, chases, and returns dated comparable prices. Second, the buyer already has a budget line in exactly this band — Anoplex publishes $150-$375/mo, Uptool starts at $195/mo — so the question is allocation, not creation. Third, the wedge is concierge-able: the builder can run it by hand for five shops this week with nothing but a model API and an inbox, which matches a nights-and-weekends operator far better than the government, city-hall or RIA candidates that all demand long procurement.

It builds on, but does not repeat, two past ideas. Promiseline (2026-11-05) chases machine shops on behalf of a *hardware startup buyer* after the PO exists. Outbound (2026-11-04) sits inside a machine shop and manages vendor POs for outside processing *after the job is won*, with the quality flowdown as the focus. Sidecar is earlier in the clock and is about money rather than paperwork: it is the pre-award price-discovery moment, where the estimator is blocked and the margin is actually set. Different trigger (an RFQ, not a PO), different output (a comparison card that goes into a bid), different failure mode (a bad guess, not a late part).

Honest limits on the score: pain is 7.5, not 9, because no survey quantifies the margin lost to stale outside-process prices — the mechanism is documented across several trade sources but the dollar figure does not exist publicly, and the validation test is designed to produce it from one shop's own POs. The biggest unmodelled risk is that Forgepoint, which already sits in the metal-finishing quoting workflow and has a16z speedrun money, turns around and serves the buyer side too.

Runner-up (Project, 7.8): Freshline beat the others because it is the only candidate where a real 2026 behaviour change (cooldowns becoming default across npm, pnpm, Renovate and VS Code) has created a question people are being told to care about — "how new is the code I'm installing?" — with no visual answer anywhere, and where the data to answer it is free, keyless and already in a file the user has open. The teardown, Cuttlefish and follower-growth candidates all died on the same rock: the thing in the bookmark already exists and is better than anything I could ship in a weekend. The secret-scanning and vibe-security candidates died on crowding. It fits the taste file's shape exactly: one input box, no signup, a result in seconds, open source, and a launch post that is mostly the screenshot. It does not overlap tonight's venture (Sidecar serves CNC job-shop estimators chasing vendor quotes; Freshline serves JS developers and shares no audience, workflow or theme). It builds on the library's "Strangers" (same lockfile input) but asks a different question with a different output and a different fix, and it must not reuse that name. could_grow is true but weakly: the honest path to a business is a CI check and an org dashboard for cooldown policy compliance, which is squarely Socket/Semgrep territory — so treat it as a free tool first. Score 7.8, dig_deeper: strong, but usefulness is capped at 7 until someone actually re-runs it twice, and shareability at 8 because I found no viral precedent for this specific output.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Sidecar — outside-processing quote-desk agent for job shops (PICK). Buyer-side of a lane two funded companies left open; cheapest path to a paid pilot.
2. AI quote desk sold to metal finishers themselves — FINALIST, then reshaped into Sidecar. Dropped as a standalone: Forgepoint ($9.8M, Oct 2026) and Steelhead ($84M, 250+ shops) already sell this exact workflow to this exact buyer.
3. DFM pre-flight for hardware-startup engineers (from @hemanthug/twentyfour26) — FINALIST. Dropped: Xometry, Protolabs, Fictiv and Hubs all bundle automated DFM into free instant quoting; no one pays for a standalone checker, and the buyer is an engineer with no budget line.
4. Multi-shop RFQ broadcaster for hardware-startup buyers — dropped at screen. AuraVMS at $4.99/user/mo, oboloo and Axya already cover the generic workflow; the price ceiling is near zero and it is adjacent to the past idea Promiseline.
5. Dev-laptop AI extension/MCP/skill inventory for mid-market (from @ScottWu46 + Jack Cable's guide) — dropped at screen as a near-repeat of past ideas SkillProof and SkillPeek, and killed on gap: StepSecurity Dev Machine Guard already ships this at a published $8/device/month, with Pillar ($9M) and Backslash ($27M) above it.
6. Mobile approval inbox for non-developer agents, across Zapier/UiPath/n8n (from @digitalocean Cuttlefish) — dropped at screen. Strong fit for the builder's UiPath skills, but it is a feature every agent platform ships natively, approval fatigue is the complaint rather than approval access, and it overlaps past ideas Ledger and Doublecheck.
7. "Plaid for government benefits" document-verification wedge for nonprofit benefits navigators (YC RFS, Gustaf Alströmer) — dropped at screen. CivicReach and incumbent case-management vendors already sit in the lane; the real buyer is a state agency with an 18-month procurement cycle, which fails the weeks-to-first-sale test for a nights-and-weekends founder.
8. AI plan-review wedge for city building departments (YC RFS "AI for City Hall") — dropped at screen. Archistar, Symbium and others already sell AI plan review to cities; also a close neighbour of the past idea Backcheck, and city sales cycles are brutal.
9. Governance/inventory for vibe-coded internal apps at SMBs (from @cursor_ai's deploy-from-Cursor launch) — dropped at screen. Superblocks and Caspio are already loudly positioned on "vibe coding sprawl", and the buyer (SMB IT) has latent pain and no budget line yet.
10. Compliance review for AI-drafted client communications at small RIAs — dropped at screen. Hadrius, Comply and Sedric all sell RIA comms surveillance with AI-content coverage; crowded, and far from the builder's domain.
11. "Cognitive debt" review gate for agent-written PRs (from @addyosmani) — dropped at screen. A philosophy, not a purchase order: no named buyer with a budget line, and it is thin variation on the past idea EvalSeed.

PROJECT
1. Freshline — lockfile → publish-date timeline + 7-day hot zone + cooldown card. PICK: real 2026 behaviour change (cooldowns everywhere), free keyless data, visual output, reason to return after each install.
2. Teardown-in-the-browser — photo of an object → interactive exploded 3D. Dropped at screen: the bookmark's own skill (elvarofficial/teardown, ~2.2k stars) already owns this, image-to-3D APIs cost $0.20-0.50/gen, and "Exploded" is already in the library.
3. Cognitive Debt Report — paste a Claude/Cursor transcript, get a score for how much you accepted unverified. Dropped at screen: no honest way to measure it, output is a lecture nobody posts, and it sails close to Addy Osmani's article rather than adding to it.
4. Mess Map — repo URL → visual map of copy-paste, dead wrappers, leaky abstractions (from /untangle-codebase). Dropped at screen: jscpd and GitDiagram cover the halves for free, and "untangle" is already a shipped product in the bookmark.
5. Secretsweep — browser-side scan of a dropped folder for leaked keys. Dropped at screen: gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning and a dozen free SaaS already do it; nothing left to add in a weekend.
6. Agent Approval Inbox — a shareable mock of "approve this migration from your phone" (from DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish). Dropped at screen: it's their product, and a demo with no agent behind it is a fake.
7. Startup Follower Race — animated 90-day X follower growth chart for startups (from @benln). Dropped at screen: no public dataset or affordable X API for historical follower counts; I would have to fabricate the data.
8. MCP/Extension Shelf — audit your installed editor extensions and MCP servers. Dropped at screen: mcp-audit, mcp-config-audit and coding-agent-audit already exist as free CLIs, and a browser page cannot read local config without the user hand-picking files.
9. Vibe-Ship Check — scan a deployed URL for exposed keys and missing RLS. Finalist, then dropped: VibeEval's Vibe Code Scanner, CheckVibe and VibeDoctor already sell exactly this, and an honest scan needs a backend.
10. Launch Lag — track how long between "describe the tool" and a live shared link, from the Cursor live-apps bookmark. Dropped at screen: nothing to measure, no data source, no output worth posting.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish (confirmed it is a mobile approve/deny console for coding agents, which killed candidate 6 as a feature rather than a product); Jack Cable's security guide (gave the concrete incident list — tampered AI coding-tool installer in the Binance chain, Shai-Hulud worm — and surfaced "inventory editor, browser and AI extensions and MCP servers" as the recommended action, which seeded candidate 5); Addy Osmani's "Critical thinking when agents do the work" (confirmed it is an essay about cognitive surrender, not a product gap — candidate 11 died here). I could not see the images or videos in any bookmark and did not guess at them.

Screening pot (6/6): one call each on dev-machine AI inventory (StepSecurity at $8/device/mo already sells it — candidate 5 dead), benefits-navigator software (CivicReach exists; buyer is a state agency — candidate 7 dead), vibe-coded internal-app governance (Superblocks owns the positioning — candidate 9 dead), machine-shop quoting (found Paperless Parts, Uptool, CloudNC, Dashnode — kept as finalist), mobile agent approvals (no cross-platform product, but approval fatigue is the complaint not approval access — candidate 6 dead), RIA AI-comms compliance (Hadrius/Comply/Sedric — candidate 10 dead).

Deep research pot (12/12): on the two surviving finalists. Pulled pricing and funding for Paperless Parts (quote-only; vendor says third-party price listings are wrong), Uptool ($195/mo, $6M seed Feb 2026), CloudNC Quote Agent ($20/mo starter), Steelhead ($84M from Mainsail, 250+ shops), Anoplex ($150/$125/$375 per month tiers), Forgepoint/Frank ($9.8M seed Oct 2026, Primary + a16z speedrun, seven-figure ARR claimed). Chased quoting benchmarks and found the honest state: a 20-35% win rate on submitted quotes and 3.8-4.5 day quote turnaround exist as vendor-published benchmarks with no survey behind them, so I did not lean on them. Checked the DFM/marketplace side (Xometry, Protolabs, Fictiv, Hubs all bundle free automated DFM) which killed candidate 3. Checked buyer-side RFQ tools (AuraVMS, oboloo, Axya, Precoro) which killed candidate 4 and simultaneously showed none of them read prints or handle spec flowdown — the first hint of the real gap. Checked finisher-side industry structure (~5,000 establishments, two-thirds under 20 employees) and finisher job postings (estimator/inside-sales roles at Aberfoyle Metal Treaters and Advanced Plating Technologies that explicitly list "follow up with customers for missing information"), which confirmed the manual loop exists on both ends.

Sharpening pot (5/5): two calls to test flipping from the finisher to the machine shop — one on whether anyone serves buyer-side OSP (nobody does end-to-end; ERPs only record a cost a human already fetched), one on Forgepoint specifically (confirmed it serves finishers as sellers, which is the side I vacated). Three calls to test the narrowed wedge: outside-process lead times (2-5 days heat treat, 3-7 plating, 25-100% expedite premiums), whether rate cards are standing or per-job (per-job for anything non-routine; finishers do not publish customer-facing schedules), and whether estimators guess (yes — prior quotes and provisional estimates, with lot minimums, rack charges and freight the named failure modes). What changed because of the pots: the idea moved from the wrong side of the transaction to the right one, and from a vague "manage outside processing" scope to the single pre-award moment where money is actually lost.

Investor signals weighed: YC W27 "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (the closest fit — this agent turns an office person into a spec-flowdown specialist), "AI for City Hall" and "Plaid for Government Benefits" (both generated candidates, both died on procurement cycle length and existing incumbents); a16z Big Ideas 2026 "The renaissance of the American factory", "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" and "Systems of record lose ground" (all three support the thesis that the value is in small industrial back offices, not in a new ERP). I deliberately did not propose any signal as the idea itself.
Sharpening (7 to 8.1): Round 1 — weak criterion: gap (6.5). The first shape was a generic "AI quote desk for metal finishing shops", i.e. sell to the finisher. Two sharpening calls killed it: Forgepoint's "Frank" (forgepoint.ai/industries/metal-finishing) is explicitly aimed at coating and heat-treat shops, raised $9.8M in Oct 2026 from Primary + a16z speedrun, reports seven-figure ARR within six months, and already extracts masking, testing and spec requirements; Steelhead has $84M from Mainsail and 250+ finishing shops with quoting built in. That gap is closed by funded players serving the same buyer with the same workflow. Change to the idea: flip sides of the transaction — sell to the machine shop *buying* outside processing, not the finisher selling it. Research then confirmed the buyer side is bare: a dedicated call on buyer-side OSP found no platform that sends one spec-correct package to multiple processors and returns comparable quotes; ERPs (Bizowie, JobPack, netray worksheets) only record a subcontract cost a human already obtained. gap 6.5 → 8.0, and market_pull 7 → 8 because the machine shop buyer has a documented software budget ($195-$750/mo precedents) and is the same persona Uptool and Paperless Parts already sell to.

Round 2 — weak criterion: pain (6.5, thin on numbers). Change: narrowed the wedge from "manage outside processing" to the single most expensive moment — the unconfirmed OSP price at quote time. Two calls tested whether that moment is real and costly. Found: trade sources name waiting on outside-process prices as the explicit bottleneck against a 24-48h quote target; heat treat is quoted at 2-5 days turnaround and plating 3-7 (one source: 5-14 business days door-to-door with expedite surcharges of 25-100%); shops do fall back to prior quotes or provisional estimates and the named failure modes are missed lot minimums, rack/setup charges and freight; OSP appears in an estimated 30-40% of jobs at many shops. What I did NOT find, and am not claiming: any survey quantifying margin lost to stale OSP prices, or OSP spend as a share of COGS. So pain goes 6.5 → 7.5, not higher: the mechanism is confirmed by multiple trade sources and the workaround (guessing, chasing by email) is documented, but no hard dollar figure exists, which is exactly what the validation test is designed to produce.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised Addy Osmani's "cognitive debt" article, Jack Cable's security guide (which produced the cooldown thread that became the pick), and the elvar teardown skill — the last one killed candidate 2 by showing the skill is already open source with ~2.2k stars. Screening pot (5/5): one check each on cooldown tooling, secret scanners, teardown/image-to-3D prior art, cognitive-debt tooling, and the X follower dataset — killed candidates 2, 3, 5, 7. Deep pot (8/8): confirmed npm-cooldown and dep-cooldown are CLIs only; confirmed Socket.dev's free web surface does not give a whole-lockfile age view; confirmed registry.npmjs.org packuments carry a per-version `time` map with no API key; confirmed download/metadata rate limits and that CORS is reported-working but not officially documented (which is why buildability is 8, not 9, and why the plan includes a fallback Worker); confirmed a Next.js lockfile is commonly 300+ unique packages, which set the batching/caching design; checked the Mess Map and vibe-ship-check finalists and found both crowded. Sharpen pot (4/4): searched specifically for a hosted lockfile freshness timeline with a shareable card (none found), for a viral precedent (none found — this is why shareability is 8 not 9), checked provenance/attestation fields as a secondary signal, and re-verified the cooldown ecosystem shipping dates. What changed: the idea moved from "another dependency audit" to "the picture of your build's age plus the exact blocked list," and gained the post-install diff.
Sharpening (7.2 to 7.8): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (5, a one-time toy: you look at your timeline once and close the tab). Change: added the post-install re-run loop — Freshline stores your last run in localStorage and on the next visit shows the diff ("3 packages entered the hot zone since Tuesday"), plus the explicit "would a 7-day cooldown have blocked these?" count that changes every time you update. Research (deep pot: perplexity on dep-cooldown/npm-cooldown and Socket.dev free surface) confirmed the existing tools are CLIs with one-shot text reports and no stored history or diff, so the returning-user angle is unclaimed. Usefulness 5 → 7 (capped at 7: I have no evidence devs actually re-run it; the loop is plausible, not proven). Score 6.6 → 7.2.
Round 2 — weak criteria: shareability and wow (both 7: a dependency audit is not inherently postable).
